panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of a well-defined brown (hyperchromic) macule on the medial calcaneus, i.e., a plantar pigmented macule, in an article titled 'Tinea nigra: A series of three cases'; the lesion is a classic tinea nigra presentation on the sole. Real human patient image, adequately lit light skin, no annotations. B: Dermoscopy of the same plantar lesion showing thin superficial pigmented spicules in a non-furrow-following pattern, the characteristic dermoscopic pattern of tinea nigra, in a tinea nigra case-series article. Real human patient image; background skin appears light; no annotations.

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a real pediatric patient showing a brown, well-demarcated pigmented macule on the left palm, matching the classic palmar presentation of tinea nigra. The article title ('The first report of tinea nigra from Iran'), the caption, and the in-text description of an asymptomatic brown macule without scale or inflammation directly attribute the lesion to tinea nigra. No subtype is specified in the caption or in-text, and no ethnicity is stated. Skin tone judged only from the visible, adequately lit palmar skin.
panels.attribution_text: Kelarestaghi et al. The first report of tinea nigra from Iran.. New microbes and new infections 2022. doi:10.1016/j.nmni.2022.101032. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Pigmented macule on the left palm.
in_text_mentions: A 9-year-old rural boy from Amol, Mazandaran, northern Iran presented with a 2-year history of a lowly growing asymptomatic hyperpigmented macules on his left palm. He denied pruritus or pain and no other parts of the body were affected. He had no relevant history of trauma or underlying disorders. On physical examination, a brown four-centimeter macula, with irregular pigmentation and shape; it had defined edges, without scales or symptoms of inflammation (Fig. 1). There was no history of a similar condition in the family.Fig. 1Pigmented macule on the left palm.Fig. 1

panels.rationale: Single-panel KOH wet-mount microscopy of lesional skin scrapings from a confirmed tinea nigra patient (article: 'The first report of tinea nigra from Iran'), showing branching septate hyphae with brownish, wavy-walled older sections—the classic dematiaceous (Hortaea werneckii) morphology of tinea nigra. Real human-patient image, no third-party indication; findings match the allowed vocabulary directly.
panels.attribution_text: Kelarestaghi et al. The first report of tinea nigra from Iran.. New microbes and new infections 2022. doi:10.1016/j.nmni.2022.101032. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
in_text_mentions: The patient's lesional skin scrapings were taken. For direct microscopic examination, the specimen was prepared in KOH 10% solution and observed under a microscope. The skin scrapings revealed numerous branching and septate hyphae of various diameters when examined under the microscope. The hyphae's apical part was hyaline, with parallel walls and regular septation. The oldest sections have a brownish color, a wavy cell wall, and irregularly distributed septa. (Fig. 2).Fig. 2KOH preparation in microscopic observation.Fig. 2

panels.rationale: Single-panel micrograph of a mycological (direct mount) preparation from a tinea nigra patient, showing brown, septate, branched dematiaceous hyphae. The article title ('Entodermoscopy in the Diagnosis of Tinea Nigra'), the caption ('Mycological examination: dematiaceous septate and branched hyphae'), and the in-text confirmation of Hortaea werneckii in culture directly attribute this specimen to tinea nigra. It is a real patient diagnostic specimen image, not a diagram, control, or third-party image, so it qualifies for the library. The classic pigmented hyphae of the etiologic agent are clearly visible; no age, ethnicity, or body site is stated for this microscopic view.

in_text_mentions: Both patients were from Porto Alegre, Brazil, and had the lesions for approximately 8 months. Mycological examination showed dematiaceous septate hyphae (Figure 3), and Hortaea werneckii was identified in culture. Both patients were treated with fenticonazole cream for 30 days and showed clinical improvement.

panels.rationale: Clinical photograph of a well-demarcated brown-black macule with speckled pattern on the left palm of a child. The caption explicitly identifies the lesion as a black macule on the left palm, and the article title confirms the diagnosis of tinea nigra presenting with a speckled pattern. The visible skin is light-toned. The speckled/salt-and-pepper pattern is a less common presentation, supporting a variant classification.

A: Dermoscopy image of the right palm of an 8-year-old girl diagnosed with tinea nigra (article title and in-text confirm the diagnosis); shows the characteristic brown spicules in a reticulated arrangement, a textbook dermoscopic feature of tinea nigra. B: Dermoscopy image of the left palm of a 5-year-old boy diagnosed with tinea nigra (article title and in-text confirm the diagnosis); shows brown spicules in a parallel ridge arrangement, a recognized dermoscopic feature of tinea nigra.

plate_findings.evidence: reticulated and spiculated pigmentation pattern with focal alignment along the dermatoglyphics and sparing of the acrosyringia

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Dermoscopy of a real patient lesion on the third toe showing the classic reticulated/spiculated pigmented pattern described for tinea nigra; article title and caption confirm tinea nigra as the diagnosis. B: Dermoscopy of a real patient lesion on the fourth toe showing similar reticulated/spiculated pigmented pattern; article title and caption confirm tinea nigra as the diagnosis.
panels.attribution_text: Cádiz-Bosch et al. Tinea nigra caused by Cladosporium halotolerans: first molecularly confirmed locally acquired case in Chile. Medical mycology case reports 2026. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Dermoscopic findings. (A) Dermoscopy of the lesion on the third toe showing a reticulated and spiculated pigmentation pattern with focal alignment along the dermatoglyphics and sparing of the acrosyringia. (B) Similar dermoscopic findings in the lesion of the fourth toe.
in_text_mentions: Digital dermoscopic examination showed a reticulated and spiculated pigmented pattern, with focal alignment along the dermatoglyphics, without involvement of the acrosyringia (Fig. 2A and B). Based on these findings, a superficial fungal infection was suspected, and mycological studies were requested.Fig. 2Dermoscopic findings.(A) Dermoscopy of the lesion on the third toe showing a reticulated and spiculated pigmentation pattern with focal alignment along the dermatoglyphics and sparing of the acrosyringia. (B) Similar dermoscopic findings in the lesion of the fourth toe.

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: "Dark brown to black macule on the lateral aspect of the third toe of the right foot"; in-text: "irregularly bordered, dark brown to black macules ... flat, mildly scaled, and asymptomatic."

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real patient clinical photograph of a dark brown to black macule on the right foot toe; the article is a confirmed tinea nigra case (Cladosporium halotolerans) and the caption/in-text describe the same acral pigmented macule, so disease attribution is strong. The finding maps to the plantar/foot pigmented macule vocabulary item, with the exact toe site noted in proposed_findings. B: Real patient clinical photograph of a similar dark brown to black macule on the medial aspect of the fourth toe of the same right foot, from the confirmed tinea nigra case; disease attribution is strong. Finding maps to the plantar/foot pigmented macule vocabulary item, with the exact toe site noted in proposed_findings.
panels.attribution_text: Cádiz-Bosch et al. Tinea nigra caused by Cladosporium halotolerans: first molecularly confirmed locally acquired case in Chile. Medical mycology case reports 2026. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Clinical presentation. (A) Dark brown to black macule on the lateral aspect of the third toe of the right foot. (B) Similar lesion on the medial aspect of the fourth toe of the right foot.
in_text_mentions: On day 0, physical examination revealed irregularly bordered, dark brown to black macules located on the lateral aspect of the third toe of the right foot and on the medial aspect of the fourth toe of the right foot (Fig. 1A and B). The lesions were flat, mildly scaled, and asymptomatic. Given their acral localization and pigmentation, a melanocytic lesion was considered in the differential diagnosis.Fig. 1Clinical presentation.(A) Dark brown to black macule on the lateral aspect of the third toe of the right foot. (B) Similar lesion on the medial aspect of the fourth toe of the right foot.
